title: Checkpoint: What Can We Know?
objective: After this level you can explain how philosophers define knowledge, where they think it comes from and how they answer the skeptic.
summary: Philosophers define knowledge, trace it to reason or experience, and answer the skeptic by suspending judgment, calling doubt self-refuting, or trusting custom and practice.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: can anyone really know anything?
cards.body: You’ve met a definition that cracked, skeptics who stopped judging, a brain in a vat and a sunrise nobody can prove. Time to line up how philosophers answer the doubter.

items.label: Pyrrhonists
points: Balance every argument and suspend judgment
Live by appearances, and find calm

items.label: Putnam
points: “We are brains in a vat” refutes itself
Words need causal links to things

cards.headline: Nyaya: the doubter talks too
cards.body: Nyaya gave a fourth answer to the Carvaka doubters. We couldn’t act as we do without inference, and a skeptic relies on generalizations the moment he speaks, using words with repeatable meanings.

cards.headline: Peirce: no fake doubt
cards.body: The pragmatists rejected doubting everything at once. In 1868 Peirce wrote: “Let us not pretend to doubt in philosophy what we do not doubt in our hearts.” Real doubt needs a positive reason. Yet he was a fallibilist: at any point inquiry is provisional, and we can’t tell how far we are from the truth.

cards.headline: Still no agreed definition
cards.body: And knowledge itself? After Gettier, epistemologists poured effort into repairing the three-part definition, especially in the late 20th century, but no analysis has been widely accepted. Some now doubt knowledge can be broken into parts at all. The question Socrates pressed in Plato’s Theaetetus is still open.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 complete
learned: How philosophers define knowledge, and why Gettier’s lucky cases broke the three-part definition.
What separates knowing by reason alone from knowing by experience, and why Hume doubted induction.
How Pyrrhonists, Putnam, Nyaya and Peirce each answer the skeptic.
What makes a belief true on the correspondence, coherence and pragmatist theories.

questions.prompt: By balancing equal and opposing arguments, Pyrrhonian skeptics reached _____.

options.label: a proof of the external world
a new definition of truth
options.rationale: That’s a different project: theories of truth such as correspondence and coherence.

questions.explanation: Equal arguments on both sides led the skeptic to suspend judgment, and then to tranquillity.

questions.prompt: Which four means of knowledge does the Nyaya school accept?

options.label: Perception, dreams, custom and prayer
options.rationale: Dreams and custom aren’t Nyaya’s pramanas.

options.label: Reason, memory, intuition and luck
options.rationale: Luck isn’t a means of knowledge.

questions.explanation: Nyaya’s four pramanas are perception, inference, comparison and testimony.

questions.prompt: How did Peirce respond to the method of doubting everything at once?

options.label: We should doubt everything even harder and more often
Doubt proves that we are brains in vats
Real doubt needs a positive reason; don’t fake it

questions.explanation: Peirce: let us not pretend to doubt in philosophy what we do not doubt in our hearts.

questions.prompt: How did Gettier’s job case challenge the justified-true-belief definition?

options.label: Smith’s belief turned out to be false
Smith had no evidence for his belief at all
Smith didn’t really believe his conclusion
It met all three conditions yet wasn’t knowledge

questions.explanation: True, believed and justified, but true by luck: so the three conditions aren’t enough.

questions.prompt: Match each answer to the doubter with its thinker.

pairs.right: Words need causal links to things

questions.explanation: The Pyrrhonists suspend judgment, Putnam says words need causal links to things, Hume says custom guides us anyway, and Peirce says no fake doubt.
